segs.text: Module five, objective one. The kinetics of a drug given outside the blood vessels. Extravascular means given outside the blood vessels; in this course that means by mouth, so the drug must be absorbed before it reaches the blood. She said, first order means that the rate depends on how much is there. An I V bolus puts all the drug in at once, an I V infusion puts it in at a constant, zero order rate, and an oral dose goes in by a first order process: first order in, first order out.

card.m: extravascular: oral, absorbed first
first order: the rate depends on the amount present
IV bolus: all at once   IV infusion: zero order in
oral: first order in, first order out

segs.text: Three amounts follow the dose: D G I in the gut, D B in the body, and D E already eliminated. The amount absorbed per hour is k a, the absorption rate constant, times the amount in the gut, so as the gut empties, the rate in falls. The amount eliminated per hour is k, the elimination rate constant, times the amount in the body, so the rate out rises as the body fills. The change in the amount in the body is the rate in minus the rate out: d D B over d t equals d D G I over d t minus d D E over d t. The rate constants, fractions per hour, stay the same, while the rates, amounts per hour, change with the amounts.

card.m: D<sub>GI</sub> → D<sub>B</sub> → D<sub>E</sub> (mg)
rate in = k<sub>a</sub> × D<sub>GI</sub>: falls as the gut empties
rate out = k × D<sub>B</sub>: rises as D<sub>B</sub> rises
{{frac:dD<sub>B</sub>|dt}} = {{frac:dD<sub>GI</sub>|dt}} − {{frac:dD<sub>E</sub>|dt}}   (rate in − rate out)
rate (mg/hr) changes; rate constant (hr<sup>−1</sup>) does not

segs.text: Because the drug enters gradually while it is also being eliminated, the plasma curve starts at zero, rises to a peak and then falls. In the absorption phase, the rising part, the rate in is larger than the rate out, though both processes are going on. She said, hear me when I say both processes are going on. At the peak, where the level reaches C max at the time t max, the rate in equals the rate out, so for that moment the amount in the body does not change. Just after the peak, in the post absorption phase, some drug is still being absorbed, but the rate out is now larger. Once the gut is empty, only elimination is left, and that is the elimination phase.

card.m: starts at zero → peak → falls
absorption phase: rate in > rate out, both going on
peak (C<sub>max</sub> at t<sub>max</sub>): rate in = rate out
post-absorption phase: rate out > rate in, still absorbing
elimination phase: rate out only

segs.text: Before it reaches the body, the tablet has to disintegrate, dissolve, cross membranes and pass through the liver, and k a combines all of those steps in one first order constant, per hour. Usually only part of the dose arrives, because some of it is eliminated before it becomes available, and the fraction that arrives is F, the bioavailability, between zero and one with no units. For an I V dose F is taken as one. F and k a are independent: the textbook notes that a higher k a does not mean more drug is absorbed, only that it is absorbed faster. She said, when you see a capital F, You should think oral.

card.m: k<sub>a</sub>: all absorption steps in one constant, hr<sup>−1</sup>
F: fraction that arrives, 0 to 1
IV: F = 1
k<sub>a</sub> up: faster, not more (F unchanged)
capital F → oral

segs.text: The absorption half-life is the time it takes for half of the drug still in the gut to be absorbed. It equals zero point six nine three over k a, so a larger k a gives a shorter absorption half-life. Stems usually give the absorption half-life, so it is turned into k a before any oral equation is used, and this line is not on the equation sheet. The textbook adds that absorption is generally complete after five to seven absorption half-lives.

card.m: t½<sub>a</sub> = {{frac:0.693|k<sub>a</sub>}}
k<sub>a</sub> up → t½<sub>a</sub> down
given t½<sub>a</sub> → k<sub>a</sub> first; not on the sheet
absorption complete: 5 to 7 × t½<sub>a</sub>

segs.text: She shows a curve and asks for the route. A curve that starts at zero, peaks and falls is oral; an I V bolus curve starts at its highest point; an I V infusion curve rises from zero to a plateau. She said, instantaneous in, first order out is our bolus, first order in, first order out is our oral. Oral input is usually first order, not always: a modified release product that releases drug at a constant rate gives a curve shaped like an infusion. Quiz three asked what is true at C max, and the key is that the rate of absorption equals the rate of elimination; the option that drug at the absorption site has become depleted describes the elimination phase.

card.m: peak → oral
highest at the start → IV bolus   plateau → IV infusion
modified release, zero order in → infusion shape
Quiz 3: Cmax → rate of absorption = rate of elimination
✗ absorption site depleted: elimination phase
